passage:
Last quarter, in the week before the audit deadline, I didn't notice my shoulders at all. Alka did. She told me later she had stopped asking me questions because I looked "ready to bite": shoulders up near my ears, neck stiff, typing as if the keyboard had insulted me. I wasn't angry with anyone. I was scared of missing the date.
It was Alka who finally asked, "Jomon, are you upset with me?" I was so surprised I laughed, and only then felt how sore my neck was.
Since then I've set a reminder every hour: stand, roll my shoulders, walk to the window and back. It sounds silly. But my neck hurts less, and I've started telling the team at the start of a crunch, "If I look grim, it's the deadline, not you."

qa.q: What does Jomon's hourly reminder say to do?
qa.a: Stand, roll the shoulders, walk to the window and back.

qa.q: What was Jomon really feeling during the deadline week?
qa.a: Jomon was scared of missing the date rather than angry, though the raised shoulders and stiff neck made it look like irritation.

qa.q: What small steps help Jomon now?
qa.a: An hourly reminder to stand and move, and telling the team at the start of a crunch that a grim look means deadline strain, not them.

qa.q: Why did Alka stop asking Jomon questions?
qa.a: Alka read the raised shoulders and hard typing as irritation, so she thought Jomon was "ready to bite" and kept away.

grounding: Shoulder tension during deadlines can be strain rather than irritation; breaks help, and a colleague misread it until they talked.

passage:
Chinmay, sit, I'll tell you about my first year as a site supervisor. I thought I knew everything then. A cement delivery came two days late, and the contractor, Mr. Kale, came shouting that his whole floor was delayed. I just lifted my shoulders, palms up, like this. As if to say, what can I do? He went red. He told my boss, "Shalini doesn't care."
And he was right, in a way. The truck was late, yes, but I had also forgotten to confirm the order. My shrug hid that.
The next morning I went to his cabin and said, "The late cement is partly my fault. I didn't confirm it. Here's the new date, and I'll call the depot myself every week." He grunted. But after that he trusted me. A shrug alone says "not mine." The words are what say "mine."

qa.q: How late did the cement delivery arrive?
qa.a: The cement delivery came two days late.

qa.q: What was Shalini feeling when she went to Mr. Kale's cabin the next morning?
qa.a: Shalini likely felt ashamed that the shrug had hidden the missed confirmation, and determined to own the mistake.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed things with Mr. Kale?
qa.a: Going to his cabin, admitting the unconfirmed order, giving a new date and promising weekly calls to the depot.

qa.q: How did Mr. Kale see the palms-up shrug?
qa.a: He saw it as not caring, which is why he went red and told the boss that Shalini doesn't care.

grounding: A palms-up shrug meant as helplessness felt dismissive because it dodged responsibility, and adding words of ownership repaired trust.

subtype: Hands behind the back in respect [Expressing]
passage:
"Why were you standing like a school monitor in front of the director?" Payal asked as they walked back to their desks.
"Like what?"
Payal clasped her hands behind her back and straightened up. "Like this. Chin up. For ten whole minutes."
Vidya laughed. "Oh. Habit. At my convent school we stood like that for the principal. Hands behind, no fidgeting. It meant, I'm listening, I respect you."
"It's sweet. But the director asked you twice to sit, and you kept standing. She looked a bit uneasy."
"Really?" Vidya's smile slipped. "I thought she'd take it as respect."
"She might. In my last office in Singapore, one manager hated it; said it felt like a military inspection."
"So what do I do? Just flop into the chair?"
"No. When a senior asks you to sit, sit. Keep the respect in how you listen."

qa.q: Where did Vidya learn to stand with her hands behind her back?
qa.a: At her convent school, where they stood like that for the principal.

qa.q: How did Vidya feel when Payal said the director looked uneasy?
qa.a: Vidya felt surprised and a little embarrassed, because the posture was meant as respect and attention. 😅

qa.q: What would you advise Vidya for next time?
qa.a: Sit when a senior invites her to, and show respect through attentive listening rather than a rigid stance.

qa.q: How might the director have seen Vidya's stance?
qa.a: The director may have read it as respectful, or as stiff and overly formal, which could explain looking uneasy when her offer to sit was ignored.

grounding: Hands behind the back before a senior can mean respect and attention, but in another setting it can seem stiff.

passage:
"Okay, team!" Nazia spread her arms wide at the head of the table. "This is an open floor. Any idea, any complaint, bring it!"
Amandeep raised a hand. "The weekend release keeps breaking. What if we shift to Tuesdays?"
"Hmm, no, weekends are fine. Next?"
Nobody else spoke.
Later, at the chai stall, Amandeep said, "Can I be honest, Nazia? The arms thing looked great. Very welcoming. But then you shut my idea in two seconds, and everyone saw."
Nazia winced. "I did, didn't I? I was so nervous about running my first meeting."
"Nervous is fine. Just, if you open your arms, open your ears too."
The following Monday, Nazia spread her arms again. When Amandeep spoke, she lowered them, sat down and said, "Tell me more. Why Tuesdays?"
Three people spoke after him.

qa.q: What did Amandeep suggest instead of the weekend release?
qa.a: Amandeep asked, "What if we shift to Tuesdays?"

qa.q: What was Nazia feeling during her first meeting?
qa.a: Nazia felt nervous about running a first meeting, which may be why she brushed off the idea so quickly despite the welcoming arms.

qa.q: What changed the following Monday, and why did it help?
qa.a: Nazia sat down and asked Amandeep to say more, so the open gesture was matched by real listening, and three more people spoke.

qa.q: How did the team experience the first meeting?
qa.a: They saw the open arms but also saw an idea shut down in seconds, so nobody else felt safe enough to speak.

grounding: A young leader's wide open arms invite the team, but the gesture only works when it comes with genuine listening.

subtype: Rubbing hands and drumming at work [Mismatch]
passage:
The co-working space was loud that evening, a birthday party at the next table and a blender screaming at the counter, and Dilnaz had only until eight to walk Sahil through the handover before her leave began.
Halfway down the second page, Sahil rubbed his palms together briskly. A minute later his fingers began drumming on the table, fast, tap-tap-tap-tap.
Dilnaz faltered. Was he eager to take over, or sick of her explaining? Either movement could go either way, and over the noise she couldn't read his face well.
"Sahil, the drumming. Am I going too slowly?"
He stopped and looked at his hand as if it belonged to someone else. "No! Sorry. The rubbing is the AC, it's freezing in here. The drumming is me being excited. I've wanted this client for a year."
She laughed, relieved, and turned the page.

qa.q: Until what time did Dilnaz have for the handover?
qa.a: Dilnaz had only until eight to walk Sahil through the handover.

qa.q: What was Dilnaz feeling when Sahil started drumming?
qa.a: Dilnaz felt unsure and a bit anxious, wondering if Sahil was impatient with her explaining, though the drumming might equally have meant eagerness.

qa.q: What did asking achieve that guessing could not?
qa.a: It showed that the rubbing came from the cold and the drumming from excitement, so Dilnaz could relax and carry on instead of rushing.

qa.q: How might Sahil have felt if Dilnaz had rushed through the handover?
qa.a: Sahil could have felt confused and short-changed, missing details he needed for a client he was excited to take on.

grounding: Rubbing hands and drumming fingers can mean anticipation or impatience, and asking works better than guessing.

subtype: Wringing hands and grief or anxiety [Interpreting]
passage:
You asked what I actually did that night at the hospital. Honestly, not much. Ritu's father was in surgery, and she sat on that steel bench twisting her hands, over and over, like wringing out a wet cloth. Her knuckles went pale. I had a whole speech ready: everything will be fine, the doctors are good, all that. But looking at her hands, I didn't think words would reach her.
So I sat. I didn't grab her hands; she hadn't asked for that. After a while I said, "Ritu, it's just me, Jaya. I'm not going anywhere. Water, or should I call your brother?" She nodded at the water. Later she said, "Call him."
Four hours. Mostly silence. When the doctor came out and said it had gone well, her hands finally went still. Weeks later she told me the quiet was what helped.

qa.q: Where did Ritu sit while her father was in surgery?
qa.a: Ritu sat on a steel bench, twisting her hands over and over.

qa.q: What did Ritu's wringing hands suggest about her?
qa.a: They suggested Ritu was intensely anxious and frightened for her father; they could also show helplessness at having nothing to do but wait.

qa.q: Which choices helped Ritu most, and why?
qa.a: Jaya sat quietly, didn't grab her hands without asking, and offered simple help like water or a call, which respected what Ritu needed.

qa.q: What would change if Jaya had given the speech about everything being fine?
qa.a: Ritu might have felt unheard or pushed to sound hopeful, and the words probably wouldn't have reached her through the worry.

grounding: Wringing hands during a hospital wait show anxiety, and quiet presence with a calm offer of help matters more than words.

passage:
Wednesday night
Greeting day, apparently. Three new people, three different hellos.
Morning: the client's finance head walked in, and I stuck my hand out like a robot. She smiled, put her palms together and said, "Namaste." My hand hung there for a second. I folded it into a namaste too, cheeks hot. She didn't seem to mind at all.
Lunch: Parul from their design team offered a firm handshake before I could decide anything. Easy.
Evening: an older gentleman from their legal team just nodded at me from across the table, hand on his chest. I nodded back and kept my hands still.
Lesson for Mehak, twenty-four and still learning: wait half a second. Let them go first. If I can't tell, I can just ask, "Handshake or namaste?" Parul said people actually like that question.

qa.q: How did the client's finance head greet Mehak?
qa.a: She smiled, put her palms together and said, "Namaste."

qa.q: How did Mehak feel when the outstretched hand hung in the air?
qa.a: Mehak felt embarrassed, with hot cheeks, though a little relieved that the finance head didn't seem to mind.

qa.q: What rule of thumb did Mehak settle on?
qa.a: Wait half a second, let the other person go first, and if unsure, simply ask, "Handshake or namaste?" 🙂

qa.q: How might the finance head have seen the moment?
qa.a: She probably saw an eager newcomer and was relaxed about it, since she smiled and didn't seem to mind the mismatch.

grounding: A young professional chooses between namaste, handshake and nod by following the other person's lead or asking.

passage:
Sudha, you asked why I put my hand on my chest when the neighbour thanked me. Let me tell you where I learned it. In the flood year I was working at the ration office in Bhagalpur. A woman came with three children, soaked, no papers. I stayed late and wrote her name in the register myself. She didn't say much. She just put her right hand over her heart, looked straight at me and bowed a little, eyes full. I still feel that.
That same month a visiting officer made the same gesture on the stage, hand on heart, while checking his watch. Nobody believed him.
Same hand, same chest. The difference was everything around it. So when your Samir Nana does it, beta, I hope you look at my eyes too.

qa.q: Where was Samir Nana working in the flood year?
qa.a: He was working at the ration office in Bhagalpur.

qa.q: What was the woman feeling when she put her hand over her heart?
qa.a: She was most likely deeply grateful and moved, shown by her steady look and full eyes; she may also have been too exhausted and overwhelmed to speak.

qa.q: What choice did Samir Nana make for the woman, and why did it matter?
qa.a: He stayed late and wrote her name in the register himself though she had no papers, which is what earned her heartfelt thanks.

qa.q: Why did nobody believe the visiting officer's gesture?
qa.a: He checked his watch while doing it, so the rest of his manner showed hurry rather than sincerity.

grounding: A hand over the heart shows thanks and sincerity, but its warmth comes from the whole manner, not the gesture alone.

subtype: Finger to lips and safety limits [Mismatch]
passage:
On Monday, visiting his aunt in the hospital ward, Kamal had seen a nurse lift a finger to her lips and nod at a sleeping patient. He had lowered his voice at once. A polite request; easy.
On Thursday, at the warehouse where he worked nights, the same gesture felt different. Farhan, the shift supervisor, had chained the rear fire exit to stop pallets going missing. When Kamal stared at the padlock, Farhan put a finger to his lips. "Not a word. We'll open it before the inspection."
Kamal's stomach tightened. Forty people worked that floor, and the front door was half blocked by boxes.
His phone was at four percent. At the end of the shift, before it died, he called the company's safety helpline and reported the chained door. By noon the site manager had come down, cut the chain and posted a notice. Farhan didn't speak to him for a day. Kamal slept better anyway.

qa.q: What had Farhan chained shut?
qa.a: Farhan had chained the rear fire exit.

qa.q: Why did Kamal's stomach tighten when Farhan signalled silence?
qa.a: Kamal felt alarmed and uneasy, because this finger to the lips asked him to hide a danger to forty people, not to keep quiet for a sleeping patient.

qa.q: What did Kamal do, and why was it right?
qa.a: He called the safety helpline before his phone died and reported the chained door, because a secret that puts people at risk should go to someone responsible.

qa.q: What would change if Kamal had kept the secret?
qa.a: The fire exit would have stayed chained, and in an emergency forty workers could have been trapped with the front door half blocked.

grounding: A finger to the lips can be a polite request for quiet or a demand to hide something harmful, and sharing a harmful secret with a responsible person is right.

passage:
Observation note, project review, Thursday
Neelam chaired her first review today. Some notes for our monthly check-in.
Early on, when Varun from logistics sat quietly, she turned an open palm towards him and said, "Varun, you've seen the depot. What do you think?" He spoke for the first time in three meetings. Good instinct.
When two engineers started talking over each other about costs, she lowered her hand slowly, palm down, and said, "One at a time, let's hear both." The room settled.
Less good: when the regional head began a long aside, she put her hand up flat like a traffic signal and said, "Let's park that." He went quiet, but his face tightened, and he left early.
Next time, I'll suggest she ask a senior, in words, whether they can move on, rather than using a stop sign with her hand. I'll also tell her how well the Varun moment went.

qa.q: What did Neelam say when she turned her palm towards Varun?
qa.a: She said, "Varun, you've seen the depot. What do you think?"

qa.q: Why do you think Neelam put her hand up flat at the regional head?
qa.a: Neelam was probably anxious about time and keen to keep her first review on track, but the sharp gesture came across as controlling to a senior.

qa.q: What does the note-writer plan to suggest for next time?
qa.a: To ask a senior in words whether they can move on instead of using a stop-sign hand, and to praise the Varun moment.

qa.q: How did Varun respond to the open palm?
qa.a: Varun felt invited and spoke for the first time in three meetings.

grounding: An open palm invites a quiet colleague and a calm hand slows a heated exchange, but a sharp stop gesture at a senior seems controlling.
